title: Project Overview
description: There is no README in this repository; GEMINI.md is the closest thing to one, describing the PHP 8.1 / MySQL stack, the pages/ layout split by role, and every external integration the app talks to (Gemini AI, Google OAuth plus TOTP MFA, PayMongo, PHPMailer, Resend, QR codes, TCPDF/FPDF). AGENTS.md sits alongside it with the engineering constraints a newcomer hits within the first hour: the router allowlist, the runtime schema mutation, and the fact that display_errors is off so fatals render as a blank page. Read both before touching code - the rest of this tour assumes their vocabulary.

title: The Single Router
description: index.php is the only authenticated entry point: every screen in the app is index.php?page=<name>. It loads config.php and functions.php, re-reads and re-validates the user from the database on every request, checks the page name against the per-role $rolePages allowlist, then resolves it through an ordered fallback chain (own role directory, then pages/<page>.php, then other role directories, then dashboard) and wraps the result in the header/sidebar/footer shell. Two consequences dominate everything downstream: files under pages/<role>/ are not standalone, because they assume the router already defined $user, $role and $page and calling requireRole() with no require_once of their own, and a page missing from the allowlist does not error - it silently redirects to the dashboard.
languageLesson: PHP's require/include is runtime file inclusion rather than a module system, so a 'route' here is just a filesystem path. The router emulates a route table with an allowlist plus an ordered fallback chain of candidate paths, which is why adding a page touches three separate files and why a typo degrades silently instead of 404ing.

title: Configuration and Environment
description: config.php is the only reader of environment state and the first file both the router and every API endpoint load. Its hand-rolled loadEnv() parses .env into $_ENV and putenv(), which is why there is no dotenv dependency; DB_* values fall back to Railway-style MYSQLHOST/MYSQLPORT variables, and APP_URL is sniffed from request headers when unset. .env.example is the documented inventory of all 18 runtime variables - MySQL credentials, VAPID web-push keys, PayMongo, Google OAuth, Gemini, SMTP and Resend. Two sharp edges to carry forward: several define()s such as GEMINI_MODEL and UPLOAD_DIR are not environment-driven at all, and base-path detection only special-cases /snaptrack, so deploying under any other subfolder breaks every generated URL.
languageLesson: The .env format is plain KEY=value lines. Most projects parse it with a dotenv library loaded through Composer autoloading; here it is reimplemented in PHP so the app can read secrets before anything else boots, with putenv() additionally exporting values to any child process or extension that reads the real environment.

title: The Shared Kernel
description: functions.php is the most depended-upon file in the graph by a wide margin, and the reason is that it is the app's entire shared surface: db(), session and currentUser(), requireRole(), the CSRF helpers, flash messages, notifications, loyalty tiers, inventory deduction and view helpers all live in this one procedural file. The decision worth understanding early is that the first db() call of every request triggers ensureDatabaseSchema(), which ALTERs missing columns and MODifies ENUMs on users, bookings, payments and packages - self-healing, so no migration file is ever needed, but also a schema that mutates at runtime and therefore needs ALTER privileges. Note that display_errors is switched off in this same file, so any fatal renders as a blank page and is written to php-errors.log instead.
languageLesson: db() sets PDO's ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES to false, which sends parameter binding to MySQL for real. Values are bound, but identifiers (table and column names) can never be bound at all - that is why every query in this project interpolates only hard-coded identifiers and passes every user value through a bound parameter or cleanInt()/cleanFloat().

title: The Data Model
description: sql/install.sql is the source of truth: eleven CREATE TABLE statements followed by seed data for studio settings, demo users, packages, inventory, bookings and loyalty cards, with comments written in Filipino. users carries the identity story that Step 6 implements, holding role and active state, lockout tracking, email verification tokens, Google OAuth linkage, TOTP MFA secrets and bcrypt-hashed backup codes. packages self-references through parent_id to model sub-packages under a main package, and bookings stores a price snapshot plus a deposit / remaining-balance split so historic totals never shift when a catalogue price changes. payments then hangs off a booking with amount, type, method, reference number, uploaded proof image and verification status - the rows that Step 10 reconciles, and any column added here must also be added to ensureDatabaseSchema() from Step 4 or fresh and migrated installs diverge.
languageLesson: This is a single bootstrap script rather than an ordered migration chain: it is not idempotent, so running it twice fails on CREATE TABLE. That is why the runtime ALTER-based upgrader in functions.php exists, and why the two representations must be edited together.

title: Accounts, Email and MFA
description: login.php is the authentication front door and unusually packs four flows into one page, with a single CSRF-protected POST handler dispatching on a hidden action field for login, register, forgot_password and reset_password. send-verification.php, required by login.php, delivers verification and password-reset mail and tries the Resend REST API before falling back to PHPMailer SMTP, because outbound SMTP ports are blocked on the Railway deployment target. mfa-helper.php wraps a dependency-free RFC 6238 TOTP implementation in an MFAHelper class - Base32 secret handling, HOTP code derivation, constant-time comparison with time-slice tolerance, otpauth:// URI building and QR rendering - and mfa-setup.php drives the four-state enrollment flow around it. Together these four files turn the users columns from Step 5 into a working login: credentials, email verification, token reset, and optional two-factor.
languageLesson: TOTP is HOTP (RFC 4226) applied to a time counter instead of an event counter: the shared Base32 secret is decoded to bytes, HMAC-SHA1 is computed over a truncated 8-byte counter, and a 6-digit code is taken from the dynamic truncation. Because both sides generate codes from wall-clock time, verification checks the current time slice plus its neighbours to tolerate clock drift.

title: Public Entry Points and OAuth
description: Everything in Step 2 happens only after a session exists; these five scripts are what a browser can reach before authentication. landing.php is the public marketing page for the self-shoot studio and branches its calls to action on whether isLoggedIn() is true and what role the session holds. The Google trio is a clean authorization-code flow: google-login.php redirects to Google's authorization endpoint, google-config.php is the single place that derives GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET and GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI from the environment (delegating to config.php from Step 3), and google-callback.php exchanges the code for a token via google/apiclient, rejects non-Gmail addresses, then auto-creates or verifies the user before regenerating the session and redirecting into the routed dashboard, with logout.php as the matching teardown. Notice how thin the shared surface is: each script requires config.php and functions.php itself rather than passing through index.php.
languageLesson: The OAuth2 authorization-code flow trades a short-lived `code` for tokens via a POST to Google's token endpoint. The redirect URI sent at the authorization step must match the one sent at the token step byte for byte, which is why all three scripts read it from one shared file instead of each composing it from APP_URL independently.

title: The Presentation Shell
description: index.php wraps every resolved page in three partials, and this is where the navigation contract lives. header.php emits the head, escapes the page title through clean() and links the one stylesheet that is actually loaded; sidebar.php hardcodes the $navAdmin / $navStaff / $navClient link tables, which must be kept in sync with the $rolePages allowlist from Step 2 or a link silently drops the user on the dashboard; footer.php closes the layout, injects the SnapBot chatbot widget and loads assets/js/app.js. assets/css/styles.css is the real design system - 52 CSS custom properties declared on :root defining the soft light-gray theme, plus responsive breakpoints - and assets/js/app.js is the thin utility layer for sidebar toggling, toasts, table filtering, modals, form validation and print sections. Beware the decoys: the root styles.css, assets/images/css/styles.css and the root app.js prototype are byte-identical or wholly unreferenced, so edit the assets/ copies.
languageLesson: CSS custom properties declared on :root are inherited custom properties, effectively design tokens: a component styles itself by reading var(--surface) rather than a literal colour, so retheming the whole app is a change in one block. The same variable cascade is what makes the responsive breakpoints at the end of the file able to retheme rather than merely resize.

title: Client Booking Flow
description: pages/client/booking.php is where the customer-facing half of the domain becomes concrete: it validates package, date, time and headcount against the studio's 10:00-19:00 window, detects schedule overlaps, then inserts the booking, an UNPAID RESERVATION payment row and a loyalty-card increment together before notifying staff. It is also the clearest illustration of the constraint from Step 2 - the file opens with requireRole('client') and carries no require_once of its own, so it is unreachable outside the router and fatals if opened directly. pages/api/check_availability.php answers the calendar's asynchronous questions with a 15-minute slot grid carrying a three-state result (available, pending approval, fully booked) in which confirmed bookings outrank awaiting-approval ones. pages/client/bookings.php handles cancellation, blocking it within a day of the shoot and on terminal statuses while cascading to unpaid and pending payment rows, and pages/client/dashboard.php assembles the loyalty card summary and next upcoming session on top of the same tables.
languageLesson: This page mixes server-rendered PHP with roughly 800 lines of inline JavaScript implementing the calendar, the slot grid and the sub-package drill-down. Because it has no require_once header it can only ever run inside the router's execution context, where $user, $role and $page are already defined - a pattern used by nearly every file under pages/.

title: Payments and Loyalty
description: Payments are the most stateful flow in the app and they cut across every role. On the client side pages/client/payments.php is almost entirely a vanilla-JS single-page app whose only PHP is the requireRole gate; it fetches everything from pages/api/client-payments.php, which serves three actions - GCash and Maribank account details from the settings table, the client's payment rows joined to bookings and packages, and a CSRF-protected submission of a proof screenshot. pages/api/record-payment.php is the staff counterpart, handling RESERVATION, BALANCE and FULL payment types, applying the loyalty discount, and writing the payment row while flipping the booking status inside a single transaction before firing client and admin notifications. pages/staff/payments.php is the verification console on top of those rows, recomputing effective price from loyalty_cards.total_bookings and handling verify, reject and refund - and one trap is worth knowing, since pages/api/check-client-loyalty.php duplicates the 2/4/7/10 tier thresholds inline instead of calling getLoyaltyTier() from Step 4, so the two definitions can drift apart silently.
languageLesson: Money lives in DECIMAL columns, never floats, and is formatted only at render time with number_format(). Where a payment row and its booking status must move together, the writes are wrapped in a PDO transaction so a failure rolls both back rather than leaving a paid record against a stale booking.

title: Front Desk Operations
description: pages/staff/ is where the daily session lifecycle actually runs. staff/bookings.php implements the full approve / complete / cancel state machine, triggering notifications and deducting inventory on completion, and models the fixed 100-peso reservation fee that record-payment.php from Step 10 also assumes. staff/walkin.php is the largest page in the batch: it ALTERs the bookings table at request time to add duration_minutes, parses package duration strings into minutes, detects conflicts, finds-or-creates the client user (issuing a random password through a notification), inserts the walk-in booking with a pending reservation payment, bumps the loyalty card, and ships about 500 lines of inline JavaScript for a month calendar with async loyalty lookup against pages/api/check-client-loyalty.php. staff/inventory.php is the stock ledger, refusing deletion while booking_inventory still references an item and calling checkLowStockAndNotify() on every mutation, and staff/upload.php handles photo delivery with a 50 MB per-file cap into UPLOAD_DIR.
languageLesson: walkin.php issuing ALTER TABLE during a normal page request is legal SQL but expensive: MySQL rebuilds the table to add a column, which locks it for concurrent readers. It is a symptom of shipping schema fixes inside page code rather than in the bootstrap SQL, and it is why the central ensureDatabaseSchema() upgrader exists.

title: Admin Analytics and AI Feedback
description: The admin portal is read-mostly oversight, and pages/admin/dashboard.php is its centre of gravity: the largest file in the project at roughly 2350 lines, two thirds of them inline CSS, computing revenue versus booked sales, walk-in versus online splits, a monthly trend capped at 24 months, top-5 packages by revenue, busiest weekday analysis and a low-stock alert list. pages/admin/reports.php layers nine report types on top with PDF and CSV export, deriving revenue from actually paid payments rather than booking totals and computing genuine period-over-period deltas. Feedback closes the loop on the domain: pages/admin/feedback.php triages reviews using analyzeFeedbackWithAI() from ai_helper.php - a raw-cURL Gemini call with a five-model fallback chain - and falls back to a local Tagalog/English keyword sentiment scorer whenever the AI columns are absent, while the client submission page applies the same tagging so urgent negative feedback escalates to staff. The pattern worth copying is graceful degradation: AI enrichment is an enhancement here, never a dependency.
languageLesson: External AI calls here use raw cURL against the generativelanguage REST endpoint rather than an SDK, with a chain of model ids tried in turn until one answers. Each call site pairs that with a deterministic local scorer, which is the general rule for third-party calls: network, quota and model deprecation all become non-fatal.

title: Build, Deployment and Ops Scripts
description: composer.json is the runtime manifest - PHP >=8.1 with the pdo, pdo_mysql and mysqli extensions, plus google/apiclient, phpmailer/phpmailer and endroid/qr-code - and notably it declares no autoload section, which is why every dependency edge in this codebase is an explicit manual require_once rather than PSR-4 resolution. nixpacks.toml is the deployment counterpart: two lines declaring the PHP extensions the build image needs, including gd, curl and mbstring that the base image omits, without which the Railway deployment cannot serve the app at all. The last stop is ops tooling that ships unguarded: sql/install.php is a browser-accessible database installer with no authentication whatsoever, and change_password.php is a one-shot script that resets every row of the users table to the literal password 'password' on a plain GET, so treat both as delete-before-production, alongside other dead code such as pages/api/get-day-bookings.php (a zero-byte stub returning an empty 200), includes/booking.php, includes/deduct_inventory.php, pages/admin/DFD.HTML and public/service-workers.js.
languageLesson: Nixpacks builds a container image from a declarative TOML file of system packages rather than a Dockerfile. Adding nixpacks.toml to extend the base PHP image with gd, curl and mbstring is the minimal way to supply extensions the stock image leaves out, and it replaces the multi-stage Dockerfile pattern entirely.
